sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Prometheus is an open-source, pull-based, multi-dimensional time-series database and monitoring system originally built at SoundCloud in 2012, now the de facto standard for cloud-native monitoring — it scrapes metrics from instrumented targets via HTTP, stores them in a local TSDB with powerful query language (PromQL), and integrates with Alertmanager for routing and Grafana for visualization.
Prometheus was born at SoundCloud in 2012 out of frustration with the existing monitoring tools — Nagios was alert-centric but had no time-series store, Graphite stored time series but had no service discovery and a weak query language, and StatsD was push-based and lossy. The SoundCloud engineers — Julius Volz and Björn Rabenstein among them — designed a system that combined the best of these: a time-series database, a pull-based scrape model, multi-dimensional labels (borrowed from Google's Borgmon), and a query language (PromQL) that could express rate calculations, aggregations, and joins. Prometheus joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation in 2016 as its second hosted project after Kubernetes, and is now the default monitoring system for Kubernetes clusters — every major cloud provider ships Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoints, and the OpenMetrics standard codifies the exposition format. Real-world deployments span DigitalOcean (which runs a multi-tenant Prometheus fleet monitoring thousands of customer clusters), CERN (which uses Prometheus to monitor the LHC computing grid), and Uber (which built M3 as a Prometheus-compatible system at planetary scale).

The first foundational concept is the pull model. Unlike StatsD or InfluxDB, which receive metrics pushed by applications over UDP or TCP, Prometheus actively scrapes targets by issuing HTTP GET requests to a `/metrics` endpoint on a configurable interval (default 15 seconds). The target responds with a plain-text exposition format — `http_requests_total{method="GET",status="200"} 12345` — and Prometheus parses, labels, and stores the samples. The pull model has three advantages over push: it is symmetric (Prometheus knows whether a target is up by whether the scrape succeeds — a missing scrape is itself an alert), it puts the operator in control of sampling rate (one Prometheus can scrape a thousand targets at 15s, another at 60s), and it eliminates the trust boundary problem of push (a misconfigured client cannot overwhelm the database by pushing too fast). The trade-off is that pull requires Prometheus to reach every target — which is fine for services but awkward for short-lived batch jobs (handled via a Push Gateway for batch metrics) and for firewalled networks (handled via federation or relays). SoundCloud's original architecture relied on pull precisely because it made the monitoring topology explicit.

The second concept is the metric type. Prometheus defines four types, each with a specific semantics: Counter (a monotonically increasing value, like total HTTP requests served — you compute a rate with `rate()`), Gauge (a value that goes up and down, like current memory usage or queue depth — you read it directly), Histogram (a distribution of values bucketed into configurable ranges, like request latency — you compute quantiles with `histogram_quantile()` over the buckets), and Summary (pre-computed quantiles on the client side, like p50/p90/p99 latency — inflexible because you cannot aggregate quantiles across instances). The choice between Histogram and Summary is the most consequential: Summary pre-computes quantiles client-side, which seems convenient but makes aggregation impossible — the p99 of two services' summaries is not the p99 of the combined distribution, so cross-instance aggregation gives wrong answers. Histogram stores bucket counts, allowing correct aggregation via `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))`. The Prometheus team officially recommends Histogram over Summary for any metric you will aggregate, and the introduction of native histograms in Prometheus 2.40 (2023) made bucket boundaries dynamic, removing the last argument for Summary.

The third concept is labels and cardinality. Every Prometheus metric is identified by a metric name plus a set of label key-value pairs — `http_requests_total{method="GET",status="200",route="/checkout"}`. This multidimensional model is what makes PromQL powerful: you can aggregate, slice, and join by any label. The cost is cardinality explosion: every distinct combination of labels creates a new time series, and Prometheus stores each series as an independent column of samples. A metric with labels `method` (10 values), `status` (60 values), `route` (500 values) creates up to 300,000 series, which is manageable. But add a `user_id` label with 260 million values and the database explodes — this is the cardinality trap, and it is the single most common cause of Prometheus outages in production. The rule, codified in every Prometheus training, is: never put high-cardinality labels (user_id, session_id, request_id, trace_id) on metrics — use logs or traces for those. The Prometheus team enforces this through the `label_keep` and `label_drop` relabeling rules and through the TSDB's own performance characteristics, which degrade nonlinearly above ~10 million active series per server.

The fourth concept is PromQL. PromQL is the query language, and it is what distinguishes Prometheus from simpler TSDBs like Graphite. The core operations are: instant vector selectors (`http_requests_total` returns the latest value of every series), range vector selectors (`http_requests_total[5m]` returns all samples in the last 5 minutes), aggregation operators (`sum by (status) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))` groups by status), arithmetic (`rate(a[5m]) / rate(b[5m])` computes a ratio), and the histogram functions. PromQL's distinctive feature is that it operates on vectors of series natively — `sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (status)` is one expression that returns one time series per status code, computed in parallel across all matching series. The query `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))` computes the p99 latency across all instances, correctly aggregated, in a single line. PromQL is not Turing-complete and has no joins in the SQL sense — the closest is `vector matching` via `on()` and `ignoring()` clauses — but it is expressive enough for the vast majority of monitoring queries.

The fifth concept is service discovery. In a Kubernetes or dynamic-cloud environment, targets appear and disappear constantly — pods are scheduled and evicted, autoscalers add and remove instances, services move between nodes. Hardcoding target IPs in the Prometheus config is unworkable. Prometheus solves this with service discovery integrations: `kubernetes_sd_configs` queries the Kubernetes API for all pods matching a label selector and rebuilds the target list every few seconds; `ec2_sd_configs`, `gce_sd_configs`, and `azure_sd_configs` do the same for cloud VMs; `dns_sd_configs` resolves SRV or A records; `file_sd_configs` reads a JSON or YAML file that an external process updates. Relabeling rules then transform discovered targets — drop unwanted labels, add metadata like environment or region, map a pod's container port to a scrape path. The combination of service discovery plus relabeling is what makes Prometheus work in dynamic environments without manual config changes.

The sixth concept is Alertmanager and federation. Alertmanager is a separate component that receives alerts fired by Prometheus (via PromQL alerting rules like `ALERT HighErrorRate IF rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) > 0.1`), deduplicates them, groups them, and routes them to receivers (PagerDuty, Slack, email, Opsgenie) with silencing and inhibition rules. Federation is the mechanism by which one Prometheus scrapes another — used to aggregate metrics from per-team or per-region Prometheis into a global view, or to expose a subset of metrics to a central monitoring system. The HA story for Prometheus itself is the thorniest part: Prometheus is intentionally not clustered — a single instance is the source of truth for its targets, and HA is achieved by running two identical instances behind a load balancer or with Thanos/Cortex/Mimir providing long-term storage and cross-instance query. The Prometheus team's official position is that single-instance reliability is high enough (with WAL replay and remote_write to a long-term store) that clustering is unnecessary for most teams, and the operational complexity of clustering outweighs the benefit.

The trade-off in Prometheus is flexibility versus scale. The pull model, the labels, and PromQL make Prometheus extremely flexible for typical cloud-native workloads — but the single-server TSDB does not scale horizontally, and at multi-million-series scale teams must shard (by service, by region, by team) or move to a federated architecture (Thanos, Cortex, Mimir). The choice is: use Prometheus for everything up to ~10 million series per server, and adopt a horizontally-scalable Prometheus-compatible system (Mimir, Cortex, Thanos, VictoriaMetrics) when you exceed that. The fact that all these systems speak PromQL means the migration is operational, not a rewrite.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant SD as Service Discovery (k8s API)
    participant P as Prometheus
    participant T1 as Target (app /metrics)
    participant T2 as Target (exporter)
    participant TSDB as Local TSDB
    participant R as Alert Rules
    participant AM as Alertmanager
    participant PD as PagerDuty/Slack
    P->>SD: list pods matching label app=checkout
    SD-->>P: [pod1, pod2, pod3]
    loop every 15s
        P->>T1: GET /metrics
        T1-->>P: http_requests_total{...} 12345
        P->>T2: GET /metrics (node_exporter)
        T2-->>P: node_cpu_seconds_total{...}
    end
    P->>TSDB: append samples
    P->>R: evaluate alert rules
    R-->>P: alert HighErrorRate firing
    P->>AM: POST /api/v1/alerts
    AM->>AM: dedupe + group + inhibit
    AM->>PD: route to PagerDuty
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+--------------------+   every 5s   +--------------------------+
|  Kubernetes API    | <---------   |  Prometheus              |
|  (service discov.) |              |  - scrape config         |
+--------------------+              |  - relabel rules         |
         |                          |  - alert rules           |
         | pod list                 |  - TSDB (local disk)     |
         v                          +--------------------------+
   [pod1, pod2, pod3]                        |
                                             | GET /metrics every 15s
         +-----------------------------------+
         |                |                  |
         v                v                  v
   +-----------+    +-----------+    +---------------+
   |  App pod  |    |  App pod  |    | node_exporter |
   | /metrics  |    | /metrics  |    | /metrics      |
   +-----------+    +-----------+    +---------------+
         |                |                  |
         +----------------+------------------+
                          |
                  text exposition:
                  http_requests_total{method="GET",
                    status="200",route="/x"} 12345
                          |
                          v
                  +----------------+
                  |  Prometheus    |
                  |  parses+stores |
                  +----------------+
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+
              |                       |
        alert rule fires         PromQL query
              |                       |
              v                       v
      +--------------+         +-----------+
      | Alertmanager |         |  Grafana  |
      | dedupe+group |         |  dashb.   |
      +--------------+         +-----------+
              |
              v
       [PagerDuty/Slack]
```

### Walkthrough
1. Prometheus queries the Kubernetes API (or EC2/GCE/DNS/file service discovery) every few seconds to rebuild the list of scrape targets matching its configured selectors, applying relabel rules to add metadata and drop unwanted labels.
2. Every 15 seconds (default), Prometheus issues an HTTP GET to each target's `/metrics` endpoint, receiving the plain-text exposition format with metric names, label sets, and numeric values.
3. Prometheus parses the exposition, appends samples to its local TSDB (a WAL-protected on-disk store with block-based compaction), and concurrently evaluates alert rules at the configured evaluation interval.
4. Alert rules fire when PromQL expressions cross thresholds; Prometheus POSTs the alerts to Alertmanager, which deduplicates, groups, and routes them to PagerDuty, Slack, or email based on labels and inhibition rules.
5. Engineers query Prometheus directly (via its HTTP API) or via Grafana dashboards that issue PromQL queries and render time-series charts; long-term storage and cross-instance query are provided by Thanos, Cortex, or Mimir.

quiz.explanation: Counter is a monotonically increasing value (resets only on process restart) — use for total counts like http_requests_total or errors_total; you compute rates with rate(). Gauge is a value that goes up and down — use for current-state measurements like memory_bytes, queue_depth, temperature, in_flight_requests; you read it directly.
